hook: A coffee machine that will pour any liquid you can name is one of the most instantly graspable ideas in the archive. The fun is in the test log: read each request and guess the outcome before you see it. Most entries are light and playful, though a couple take a sudden dark turn, one of them ending in a suicide.
whyItMatters: It is a textbook example of the open-ended object, where the pleasure comes from watching researchers probe the rules one request at a time. Its break-room setting gives it a slice-of-life charm that balances heavier files, and entries that reach into other objects' files show how small crossovers make the archive feel connected.
thingsToNotice:
The machine answers intent and wordplay rather than chemistry, and the opening incident proves it: an agent orders "a cup of Joe" and collapses as the cup fills with blood, tissue and fluids matching his own DNA. Later tests confirm it can pull liquids from a distance, read memories to serve someone's favourite drink with a photo of the moment printed on the cup, and even dispense a patient's leukemia, which drains the disease only for it to return two weeks later.

The log keeps hinting at limits and motives: "OUT OF RANGE" for other dimensions and dead people, and an agent's theory that a burst of medical knowledge during a breach was the machine protecting itself. The darkest entry is the shortest: a subject asks for the perfect drink, gets an odorless lavender liquid, and soon kills himself, leaving a note saying everything since has been a letdown.

related.note: She is the one asked to judge a drink that the machine prints onto a cup instead of pouring.
A request for its secretion lines up exactly with a breach in its own containment.
